adjudicated.jp: 「おい、太一」
adjudicated.en: Sakuraba: "Hoy, Taichi."
comments: This beginning part is, besides the troll and the first warning that Taichi isn't "right" yet (and will never be, for that), a very good test of reading comprehension. Being able to spot all the parts of the story and flashback this is made up from, and most importantly how Taichi has modified them, gives an excellent reading key for exactly the kind of similarities, overlaps, and connections that need to be made throughout. If you 'get' how this is just a riff on the same verse, you might 'get' the harder parts of this. -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: Hoy is an attested attention-getter. Its archaic register is questionable, but it is not a secure source-side substitution.
adjudicated.remedy: Optional idiomatic or grammatical revision; no confirmed source-bound correction is established.

comments: Really weird line. Adapted the joke to another erroneous kana splitting, should at least sound equally bizarre and the point doesn't seem to be in the letter anyway. If there's any, it's how the oarfish is the King of Herrings; I strongly suspect Tanaka is implying this is a very big, and very red one. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Neolithic_Orkney - no relation between it and oarfishes that I can find.

Except! One of the most famous ruins of neolithic orkney is Skara Brae, which featured in both The Bard's Tale and Ultima, both classic RPGs. One of the developers of both also worked on Wizardry, which was so popular in Japan it had Japan-only sequels and inspired the author of Dragon Quest. Reaching, but only so much given how much Taichi seems to be into this. -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: The English changes the precise long-name/oarfish comparison, but it intentionally substitutes another bizarre segmentation of the same English place-name and keeps the giant-oarfish frame. Whether that replacement is successful is debatable; it is not a confirmed absence of the source’s word-soup mechanism.
adjudicated.remedy: A stronger adaptation would keep the place-name sounding like the name of an oarfish rather than making the fish speak it.

comments: See the top, that's why he can't understand the script Sakuraba wrote. And therefore, the real difficulty in understanding all the VN. It's actually easier to do so as a foreigner, paradoxically enough: the less you're bound to the conventions of read Japanese, the easier it is to notice how much Tanaka hides in plain sight. -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: The Japanese says that memories were shredded even as he formed them and mixed with other language until he could no longer judge them. The English changes remembering into deliberate memorization, pluralizes 'language,' and joins the result with an ungrammatical 'that.'
adjudicated.remedy: As soon as I formed a memory, it was torn apart and mixed with other language until I could no longer make sense of it.

adjudicated.assessment: The Japanese marvels at what had lain hidden in the heart he thought insignificant. The English front-loads the object without a relative marker and joins an exclamation to it with a coordination that never forms a complete sentence.
adjudicated.remedy: What could have been hidden in this heart of mine that I had thought so small?

highlights.text: This heart of mine I thought so tiny, yet what a thing was kept hidden within.

adjudicated.jp: 人捜しの長い旅に疲れ果て死ぬとき、はじめて振り返ると捜し人が無言でついてきていて、にっこりとほほえみかけてきたような。
adjudicated.en: It's as if you're dead exhausted after a long voyage in search of someone, and then the very first time you turn around there the person you were looking for was, wordlessly following you, grinning into a smile.
comments: How I wish that is what it felt to analyze this. Ugh. -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: The source likens the feeling to reaching death exhausted by a long search, only then looking back and finding the sought person silently following and smiling. 'Dead exhausted' turns actual dying into an intensifier, the tense shifts from present 'you turn' to past 'was,' and 'grinning into a smile' distorts the gentle smile.
adjudicated.remedy: As if, when I finally died exhausted from a long journey searching for someone, I looked back for the first time and found them following silently behind me, smiling.

highlights.text: It's as if you're dead exhausted after a long voyage in search of someone, and then the very first time you turn around there the person you were looking for was, wordlessly following you, grinning into a smile.

adjudicated.assessment: 肯定される means that everything feels accepted or affirmed without condition. The English instead says events or things undergo a change into the abstract property 'positive.'
adjudicated.remedy: everything might be accepted unconditionally

adjudicated.jp: 気がつくと、俺は闇の中でも母を見ることができるようになっていた。

When I came to notice, I seemed to have

comments: He just finished using the very word 'darkness', kanji and all, to describe his mother's fear. That's what his eyes actually allow him to see, the truth of people below what they seem to be - just what he says Kiri can do. Like the script all the way above, though examples of Taichi telling the truth without telling it are nearly everywhere. Note that "and then I noticed". -GHS

adjudicated.jp: 生後数ヶ月、中脳皮質系から視覚皮質に神経系が切り替わり、外界に適するための末梢機能が発達する時期。

A few months after birth, the central nervous
system switches over completely from the
mesocortical pathways to the visual cortex,
a period of time taken for the development of
peripheral functions suitable for the outside
world.
comments: And here begins the final scientific troll of Cross Channel... though not the last one. See book. -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: The Japanese describes a developmental period when neural processing switches from a midbrain-cortical system to the visual cortex and peripheral functions develop for adaptation to the outside world. The English changes the subject to the entire central nervous system, adds 'completely,' and makes the period itself something 'taken for' development.

comments: See CCZAS. This doesn't make literal sense, as the sheets aren't moving, and if they were, the thumbtack would either move with them, or tear them apart as they move away. The metaphor works if considered laterally: it's a sheet of paper containing a Settei pinned onto a moving reality. And you thought elephants on a turtle was odd. -GHS

The metaphor he made up about something he all but states he doesn't understand, because there's no way he can understand since he physically has no means to? Being it's a religious metaphor, of course, the answer is neither. One more thing that's not been considered so far: staring too much at computers (or reading in general) will kill your eyesight, slowly; that's why all the reading and gaming is making him like this, as in at least one meta-explanation, he's also an stand-in for the hikikomori readers of VNs and such. -GHS
